newsitem.title: UK: UK global trade gap seen yet to feel pound's pinch.
newsitem.headline: UK global trade gap seen yet to feel pound's pinch.

text.p: Britain's trade gap with the rest of the world is expected to have held steady in May, showing few signs of deterioration due to the pound's strength.
A Reuter survey of economists forecasts a global trade gap of 960 million stg in May, virtually the same as April's 961 million shortfall.

Trade with countries outside the European Union is forecast to have produced a deficit of 597 million pounds in June, a little wider than May's 563 million gap. The figures will be released at 0830 GMT on Thursday.
Michael Saunders, UK economist at Salomon Brothers, said recent figures have shown no sign of export volumes being hit by the super-strong pound.
"We doubt that clear evidence will emerge for several more months," he said. "Nevertheless, exports are likely to weaken sharply around the end of this year."
Sterling has shot up more than 25 percent on a trade-weighted basis in just less than a year, pushing up exporters' prices.
So far, the J-curve effect has not unwound so the boost to the trade balance in value terms, as export prices rise but demand is slow to react, has not worn off. But it will soon.

Saunders said April trade data showed sharp monthly gains for both imports and exports from EU countries, and he expected a fallback in both in May if the April figures are not revised. EU exports rose 1.6 percent in April while imports leaped by 8.1 percent.
David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders, agreed. "We are assuming April's surge in imports from the EU will have unwound somewhat during May." He forecast a global trade gap of one billion pounds.
Analysts at HSBC James Capel pencilled in a similar deficit and said the surprising strength of exports was a function of a pick-up in world trade growth.
"Although the UK may be losing market share, the pick-up seems to be significant enough to keep exports ticking over," they said in a client note.
If that continues, the pound's strength may not apply the brake on British economic growth that many economists expect, they said.
As for the non-EU figures, they may be more timely, reflecting June's rather than May's trade. But they offer less clues about the damage the pound is wreaking.

Philpotts said the non-EU trade gap would stick at around 500 million pounds. "But sterling has appreciated far less against these countries than it has against Europe whilst, apart from the Middle East, their markets have also been much more buoyant of late," he said.
